data.title: Canary Release
data.tagline: A canary release exposes a new version to a small amount of real traffic before health signals decide whether to expand or stop.
data.learningOutcome: You can state a canary's initial traffic, observation signals, expansion gate, and stop action.
data.description: Checkout v2 can serve 5% of requests while stable v1 keeps the other 95%; if v2 crosses its error threshold, its traffic returns to v1. This limits exposure to a release version. It is not merely switching one feature on or off inside the same release.

learning.assumes: You know old and new versions of one service can run at the same time.
learning.outcome: You can state a canary's initial traffic, observation signals, expansion gate, and stop action.

distinctions.label: Feature flag
distinctions.explanation: A Canary Release routes a small share of production traffic to a new release version. A Feature Flag can route selected people to a feature path without changing the deployed version.

explanation.title: Limit possible impact to a small scope
explanation.text: An all-at-once checkout release exposes every request to unknown defects. Giving v2 5% of traffic while verified v1 keeps the other requests tests the new release under real conditions without immediately widening impact.

explanation.title: Let agreed signals decide the next step
explanation.text: Define an observation period, error or latency threshold, and return action before release. Expand only while signals are healthy; stop and restore the stable version above the threshold. A quiet small sample still cannot prove every path is correct.

data.boundary: Progressive or gradual rollout is the broader family; a canary release specifically validates a new version with a small amount of real traffic. A feature flag routes feature paths inside a deployed release, while a canary routes production traffic between release versions. They can work together but are not identical.

lessonPractice.title: Checkout v2 is serving 5% of traffic, but its error rate reaches 7%, above the 2% threshold. What should happen next?

options.label: Stop expansion, return v2 traffic to v1, and confirm error rate and checkout success recover
options.feedback: Correct. The canary produced failure evidence, so limit impact first and verify recovery on the stable version.

options.label: Expand to 100% anyway and wait for a larger sample
options.feedback: The signal already crossed the agreed threshold; expanding would expose more people to the faulty release.

options.label: Keep 5% traffic indefinitely because the deployment job succeeded
options.feedback: A successful deployment only proves the version is running; it does not override error evidence from real traffic.

data.agentPrompt: Canary checkout v2 at 5% traffic and observe checkout error rate and latency for 15 minutes. Expand only while error rate stays below 2%; above the threshold, stop and return traffic to v1. Report actual traffic and metrics for both versions.
